newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Russian general sees no imminent Abkhazia pullout.
newsitem.headline: Russian general sees no imminent Abkhazia pullout.

text.p: President Eduard Shevardnadze sent his defence minister to Moscow on Thursday to consult on the future of Russian peacekeepers in Georgia while a top Russian military official said a pullout was not imminent.
A defence ministry spokesman said Vardiko Nadibaidze left for Moscow to meet Russian defence minister Igor Sergeyev and Armed Forces Chief of Staff Anatoly Kvashnin.

The mandate for the 1,500 strong force stationed between Georgia and its breakaway region of Abkhazia expires on Thursday. Observers fear their withdrawal could reignite the 1992-93 war between the sides that killed 10,000 people.
The peacekeeping force, known as the CISPKF, is made up of Russian servicemen but is serving under the auspices of the Commonwealth of Independent States grouping 12 former Soviet republics.
Georgia has refused to renew a mandate for the mission, saying it has not taken up new functions as ordered by the Commonwealth summit in March.

Shevardnadze, keen to head off conflicts with influential nationalists at home and but also to avoid a new war, wants a decision on the CISPKF's future put off until a September meeting of Commonwealth leaders.
A top Russian military official indicated no pullout of the CISPKF was imminent and echoed Tbilisi's position that their withdrawal could only be effected by a Commonwealth decision.

"Formally the mandate of the peacekeepers ends today, but that does not mean that tommorrow they will not be there," Itar-Tass news agency quoted Lieutenant General Alexander Arinakhin, assistant to the Russian Chief of Staff as saying.
Arinakhin said that a special decision of the Commonwealth summit, due to meet later this year, was needed for the peacekeepers to be withdrawn.
Georgian wants the force to take up an expanded remit -- policing more of Abkhazia and resettling refugees -- in return for renewing the mandate.

But Russia has rejected this, saying the Abkhaz must agree as well. The separatists are bitterly opposed, calling it an attempt to encroach on their territory. Abkhazia's de facto sovereignty has never been recognised abroad.
Russian-Georgian relations have never fully recovered from Tbilisi's charges that Moscow gave the separatists much-needed military hardware and logistical support during the war.
Shevardnadze travelled abroad earlier this month lobbying for an international force to replace or complement the Russians. But categorical Abkhaz opposition to the idea has left it a dead letter.
The Russian peacekeeping force commander told Reuters last week new fighting was probable if he and his men left the buffer zone, which they have patrolled since 1994.

About 50,000 ethnic Georgians have returned to the so-called "security zone" since the Russians took up their positions, but some fear they might have to flee again if there is a pullout. Georgian refugees from the rest of Abkhazia have not been able to return.
Peace talks between the sides are deadlocked, with the separatists wanting more sovereignty than Tbilisi will tolerate.
